source.title: Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in CLIP
source.authors: Yossi Gandelsman; Alexei A. Efros; Jacob Steinhardt

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports qualitative evidence that some CLIP neurons have multiple, sometimes unrelated concepts, which challenges the broad one-main-job proposition, but it does not test any listed version's specific model or measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper measures and decomposes CLIP neurons' second-order effects. Its qualitative sparse-decomposition examples bear on polysemanticity. It does not measure the Qwen audit shares, test InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron, estimate an interpretable-neuron share, test neuron-based attribution graphs, or score explanations by predicting activations on held-out text. Other reported results, including image selectivity, reconstruction accuracy, adversarial-image success and segmentation, do not measure the claimed job-count shares.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any listed version. It studies OpenAI ViT-B-32 CLIP (with some ViT-L-14 ablations), not Qwen3-32B, other language models or InceptionV1. It reports no share of neurons with one or several jobs: its polysemanticity evidence is 8 hand-picked layer-9 neurons (Table 2, Table 5). It does not score explanations by predicting activations on held-out inputs and builds no neuron-based attribution graphs. Calling CLIP neurons 'superposition of multiple interpretable features' is an interpretation of a related construct: what a neuron's second-order output direction decomposes into. It is not a measured rate bearing on V1–V7. The record's T5 is too strong, because no version's model or measure is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that direct and indirect effects fail to capture CLIP neuron function, and introduce a second-order lens. They find these effects sparse (significant for under 2% of images) and approximately rank-1. Decomposing them into sparse text sets shows neurons tied to multiple, often unrelated concepts, which they read as superposition. They then use this to mass-produce semantic adversarial images and for zero-shot segmentation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes second-order effects in CLIP vision-transformer neurons and decomposes their directions into sparse text representations; it does not conduct a neuron-pole audit or test explanations against held-out activation examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Sparse descriptions are drawn from different text pools and evaluated at different set sizes; the paper reports that full descriptions outperform single words at smaller set sizes, with the gap narrowing at larger sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: In ViT-B-32 CLIP layer 9, sparse text decompositions of selected neurons' second-order effect directions include multiple, often unrelated concepts (e.g. yacht and cabriolet). The paper reads these as polysemantic superposition. The evidence is qualitative and covers 8 shown neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some CLIP vision-transformer neurons' output (second-order) effects correspond to multiple distinct concepts rather than one.

fits_no_version.finding: Each neuron's second-order effect is significant for fewer than 2% of images. It is approximately rank-1: reconstructing it from the first principal component costs negligible ImageNet accuracy (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CLIP neurons' second-order effects are highly selective and roughly one-dimensional in output space.

record.problems: The neuron-polysemy evidence consists of qualitative sparse-decomposition examples from selected neurons, not a population estimate of how many neurons have one or multiple jobs. The paper does not test whether the text descriptions predict firing on held-out inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. The paper's image-selectivity, reconstruction, adversarial-generation, and segmentation results do not measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares (about 90% one job, 7% two, 2–4% unknown).
Shares in other language models, dense or mixture-of-experts, and at scale. A vision transformer (CLIP) is not a language model.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and whether such neurons detect a coherent shared feature such as pose.
Whether the interpretable-neuron share rises with better tools and architectures. No share is estimated for any model or tool.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining a large model's behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict firing elsewhere. Text decompositions are checked only by reconstruction accuracy and visual match to top images.
Automated scoring of explanations by simulating activations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: I lowered the record's T5 'tests' to 'discusses'/T6. No version's model, measure or population share is examined. The polysemanticity evidence is a handful of chosen neurons with no count or rate, so it cannot bear on the share-based versions V1, V2 or V4. It measures output-direction decompositions rather than activation-based explanations, so it does not bear on V6 or V7. Table 2 includes negative-coefficient texts, which the rows list as concepts without their sign.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B audit shares and neuron-pole job counts.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
The canonical InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and the claim that it detects a coherent shared feature rather than superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tool quality explains changes in interpretable-neuron share, including the estimates for InceptionV1-sized models.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain its behaviour without a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
